reasoning: The study generated original research data: new 11C-PBR28 and 18F-flortaucipir PET scans, MRI, and neuropathology data collected from svPPA patients and healthy controls specifically for this research (D1). The authors used existing third-party software tools (FreeSurfer, PMOD, SPM12, MATLAB curve fitting toolbox, IBM SPSS) only as utilities for processing/analysis, with no claim of having created or significantly extended any software (S2).

The paper reports an original spectroscopic host-galaxy redshift survey (3147 new redshifts collected via Hectospec, APO, WIYN, AAT observations) and PS1 photometric SN light-curve data, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1). It also describes creating its own implementation of the BEAMS method (code for solving for SN Ia/CC SN distances, combined with existing tools like SNANA and emcee), explicitly stating "Our code is available online" with a GitHub link to their BEAMS implementation—this is self-authored research software beyond merely using existing packages, satisfying S1. Per the general rule, generated artifacts subsume used ones, so the paper is classified S1D1.

The paper reports an original experiment generating new research data (genotyping results, erythrocyte/leukocyte profiles, immunological assay data from cattle infested with ticks), which is clearly D1 since it is primary data collected/generated for this research. For software, the paper only uses R and the "mgcv" package to fit generalized additive models for statistical analysis — this is generic statistical software used as a utility (akin to Excel/STATA) rather than research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so this falls under S3 (no claim of software creation or extension, and software used only as a processing utility, not as a research contribution in itself).

This is a theoretical/conceptual paper that analyzes the literature on bureaucracy and the Balanced Scorecard, constructing a conceptual matrix mapping nine bureaucracy concepts to BSC features based on literature review. The authors explicitly state the paper offers no empirical support and is a basis for future empirical research. There is no research data (no surveys, interviews, measurements, or datasets collected or used) and no research software created or used. Hence S3D3.

This is purely a literature review on energy storage for water desalination systems powered by renewable energy. It synthesizes and discusses findings from numerous prior studies, but the authors themselves do not create or significantly extend any research software, nor do they create or use any research dataset (the "Data Availability Statement: Not applicable" confirms no data was generated). Citations to other researchers' experiments/simulations are not the paper's own generated/used software or data. Hence no software and no data.

The paper uses existing research software (Weka, JADBio, and the previously published SANN method) to analyze data — no new software is claimed as created or significantly extended in this paper (S2). However, in addition to reanalyzing a previously published 192-case AAA dataset, the authors collected new primary data for their novel autism screening questionnaires (questionnaire responses from 30 patients for the first tool and 18 patients for the second tool), which constitutes newly generated research data (D1).

The paper develops a novel hierarchical EMS control algorithm (HLEM with MILP optimization, ANFIS forecasting, and the RTPC with adaptive autoregression) and implements it as custom scripts/control software in MATLAB and LABVIEW to run the optimization and control the real BESS — this is research software created for the research (S1), going beyond use of the generic MATLAB/LABVIEW platforms themselves. The authors also generated new research data: they built a laboratory microgrid testbed and performed real-time experiments, producing original measurement data (actual power drawn, SOC curves, forecasted vs. actual load/PV profiles, timing measurements) that did not exist prior to this study, in addition to using some existing third-party data (PVOutput.org PV data, SODA weather data, CREST-modeled load profiles). Since the paper both uses and generates data, the "generated" category takes precedence, giving D1.

The study generated new research data: raw multi-track sound recordings and 360° video collected in Peace Gardens, Sheffield, plus original questionnaire survey data (SQE/LoW responses) from 120 participants, which qualifies as data generated (D1). For software, the paper only uses generic/widely-established tools as utilities—SPSS and Matlab for statistical/clustering analysis and Adobe Audition for audio editing—none of which are claimed as a research contribution or are bespoke research software, so this falls under S3 (no research software).

The study generated new behavioral observation data by collecting CCTV footage and coding ethogram-based behavior data on two binturong, which is clearly research data generated (D1). No research software was created or used as a contribution; R and Excel were only used as generic utility tools for statistical analysis and data entry, which falls under "No Research Software" (S3) per the criteria's exclusion of generic statistical/processing software.

The paper is a post-hoc secondary analysis of pre-existing SSaSS trial data (collected during the original trial for cardiovascular outcomes), so the data is used rather than newly generated by this study. Only SAS, a generic statistical software package, was used for analysis, which per the criteria does not count as research software and is excluded as a utility tool (S3). Hence classified as S3D2.

The study acquired new EEG-fMRI, clinical, SEEG, and surgical outcome data from 10 (of 35) consecutive focal epilepsy patients collected 2013-2017 specifically for this research, constituting generated research data (D1). All analyses relied on existing, established research software (SPM12/DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, SEEGA, ICN_Atlas) that was used as-is for processing/analysis, with no claim of creating or significantly extending any software tool, so this is S2 (software used) rather than S1.

This is a narrative review synthesizing findings from previously published GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on type 2 diabetes and cancer genetics. The authors do not generate new research software (no tools/code/scripts are created) or new research data (no new experiments, cohorts, or datasets are produced); they only discuss and interpret statistics/findings derived from existing published studies' data. This constitutes use of existing research data (D2) with no software contribution claimed (S3).

The paper proposes a conceptual "agile smart lean-green" model and validates it via two real-world case studies (automobile and mining machinery plants), where the authors collected original production data (lead time, uptime, ergonomics, environmental issues, etc.) through Gemba walks, brainstorming sessions, and interviews with staff. This constitutes research data generated through fieldwork (D1). There is no research software created or used—mentions of "design software to decide optimum path planning" are listed only as a suggested future action, not software actually developed or employed in the study, so this is S3.

The paper analyzes life satisfaction and subjective wealth adaptation using the Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS), an existing panel dataset the authors did not create—this constitutes use of existing research data (D2). The paper performs standard fixed-effects and ordered logit regressions but does not claim to create or significantly extend any research software; the one mention of "Stata" is only within a bibliographic reference to another paper's methodology, not a description of software used/developed in this study. No research software contribution is claimed, so it falls under S3 (No Research Software).

This is a pure mathematics paper presenting theorems and proofs on matrix symmetry decomposition, illustrated with worked numerical examples (e.g., the well-known Wilson test matrix). There is no mention of any research software being created, extended, or used (calculations are illustrative hand/numeric examples, not tied to a claimed software contribution or tool), and the paper explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article," confirming no research data was generated or used.

The paper runs an "extensive suite" of numerical rotating-convection simulations (68+ simulations) to generate new simulation outputs (temperature gradient profiles, velocity fields, Brunt–Väisälä frequencies), which constitutes generated research data (D1), explicitly stated as available from the corresponding author on request. The simulation code itself is not newly created or significantly extended by this paper—it is explicitly described as pre-existing: "The code used to model the core dynamics is described in Willis et al.55" (a 2007 paper), indicating use of existing research software (S2) rather than S1. Utility tools mentioned (VisIt, Matplotlib, seaborn) are plotting/visualization tools and don't count as research software contributions.

The study analyzes a pre-existing public dataset (NABEC long-read sequencing samples, accessed via AnVIL) rather than generating new research data; findings/statistics (SV frequencies, novel insertion characterizations) are derived from this existing data, which fits D2 (data used). The authors use a range of existing third-party bioinformatics tools (Napu/Sniffles2 pipeline, Ensembl, EMBOSS/Transeq, FASTA, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, Figtree) and generic statistical/plotting R packages (RIdeogram, Plotrix, tidyverse), with no claim of creating or significantly extending any software, fitting S2 (software used).

The paper derives estimates of severe MERS cases using existing surveillance/traveler data (WHO reports, traveler case counts, trip-length data, population sizes) and statistical formulas/profile-likelihood CIs; no new dataset is created, just statistics derived from existing data sources, which fits D2 (Data Used). No research software is developed or named as a contribution—calculations and sensitivity analyses are performed using a stated formula, not a claimed software tool, and no generic tools are described as a contribution, fitting S3 (No Research Software).

The paper reports original fieldwork/observational data: shark bycatch specimens collected and examined, copepod specimens dissected, and new histological sections/images prepared and analyzed—this constitutes research data generated by the study (measurements/observations from fieldwork and histological analysis). No research software is mentioned as created or used; only standard lab equipment (autostainer) and generic preservation/histology techniques are described, none of which constitute research software.

The paper isolates, sequences, and characterizes 44 new lytic flavobacterial phages (genomes, taxonomic classifications, metagenome datasets), which constitutes generated research data (D1). For analysis, the authors use numerous pre-existing bioinformatics tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, GRAViTy, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLASTN, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, Geneious, ARB, RAxML, MiGA) without claiming to have created or significantly extended any software, so this is Software Used (S2).

The paper conducts an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study, generating synthetic datasets under various model misspecification scenarios to evaluate the LM/GS tests — this constitutes generated research data (D1). It also applies the tests to an existing real dataset (Miller et al., 1984), which counts as data used, but per the taxonomy's rule, generation supersedes use. For software, the authors rely on existing tools (R's "optim", "NumDeriv" package, and the "ltm" R package for model estimation) rather than developing and contributing new research software themselves, so this is S2 (software used) rather than S1.

The paper describes the creation of the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, a novel online software tool (built under contract, co-owned by Cool Farm Alliance/CLM/University of Cambridge) representing a clear research software contribution (S1). The research also generated substantial new research data through structured expert elicitation and evidence-assessment processes (judgement and evidence scores for hundreds of actions and species groups across biomes, provided in Supplementary Table S12), as well as real-world farm input/output data used to demonstrate the tool. This constitutes generated research data (D1), since the scoring dataset was created/derived through the research process itself, not merely sourced from elsewhere.

The paper generates original research data (PXRD, DSC, FTIR spectra, dissolution profiles) from solid dispersions the authors prepared, which constitutes data generation (D1). Software mentioned (EVA, TA Universal Analysis, OMNIC) are instrument-bundled analysis/plotting utilities used only to process data, not created or contributed as research software, and no other software use is claimed, so this is S3.

This is a humanities/architectural history article analyzing archival materials (letters, exhibition catalogues, committee reports, photographs) held at institutions like the RIBA and National Art Library. These are literature/archival sources used for historical argument, not research data as defined (no measurements, surveys, digitized datasets, or model outputs generated/restructured by the author). No research software is created or used. Hence S3D3.

This is a scoping review that synthesizes findings from existing published studies (literature), which is explicitly excluded from the definition of research data. The authors used generic tools (Excel worksheet, EndNote for deduplication) which are utility/general-purpose software, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors. No primary research data or research software was generated or used.

The paper reports a novel crystal structure determination, generating new research data (atomic coordinates, bond geometry, hydrogen-bond parameters, CCDC deposit 1537099). This counts as data generated (D1). The software used (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) is existing third-party crystallography software used only as utilities for data collection/structure solution/refinement/visualization, not created or significantly extended by the authors, and not claimed as a research contribution in its own right, so this is S3.

The paper generates new research data by conducting focus groups and semi-structured interviews with 22 teachers, which were recorded and transcribed (D1: data generated). NVivo was used only as a generic qualitative data analysis utility for coding, not claimed as a research contribution, and no other research software was created or used as a contribution in its own right (S3: no research software).

This is a literature review on protein–ionic liquid interactions. The authors did not create or use any research software themselves (all simulation/computational references are to other researchers' work cited in the literature, not performed by the authors) — S3. However, the paper compiles and synthesizes existing experimental data (e.g., solubility measurements) from the literature into summary tables (Tables 1-3), using existing research data to support its findings, without generating new data — D2.

The paper is a qualitative interpretive case study of Ach. Brito, collecting original empirical material (25 interviews, non-participant observations, archival and document research, secondary press data) over a longitudinal fieldwork period from 2007-2014. This constitutes generated research data (D1). There is no mention or claim of research software being created, extended, or used (even as a utility like qualitative coding software); the analysis is described as interpretive content analysis without any named tool, so this is S3.

This is an experimental physics paper reporting new optical/ODMR measurements (PL spectra, g2(τ) correlation data, ODMR spectra) on hBN defects, explicitly stating "datasets generated as part of the current study" — clear generation of research data. The "codes used for the analysis" are mentioned only in a generic data-availability-style statement with no claim of creating or significantly extending research software; they appear to be utility scripts for fitting/plotting data (Lorentzian/exponential fits, spin-Hamiltonian simulations) rather than a software contribution in their own right, so this falls under S3 (no research software) per the criteria for utility-only code.
